  • 揭露近年台灣人赴日涉入跨國詐騙與走私毒品的最新趨勢與驚人增長數據。
  • 深入解析跨國犯罪集團為何特別鎖定台灣年輕人作為「免洗工具人」的手段與心理盲點。
  • 了解海外違法對個人法律後果、高齡受害者家庭以及未來台灣人赴日觀光入境審查帶來的嚴重衝擊。

摘要

台灣人赴日犯罪激增：從觀光熱潮到跨國詐騙

作者指出，台灣人熱愛前往日本旅遊，但近年卻出現越來越多以觀光名義赴日從事詐騙的案例。光是近兩個月就至少發生四起台灣人涉案事件，金額從數百萬到數千萬日圓不等。根據外交部統計，台灣人在日本涉及詐騙的人數從2023年的4人暴增至2025年的50人。許多嫌犯受到網路上「海外打工兼旅遊、邊玩邊賺錢」的廣告吸引，甚至誤信「外國人被抓不會有事」的謊言，淪為犯罪組織的棋子。

犯罪集團的盤算：為何台灣人成為「闇黑打工」首選目標？

作者分析，幕後主謀涵蓋日本黑道、中國犯罪團夥以及自台灣轉移陣地的詐騙集團。日本因高齡少子化與政府強力宣導，本土犯罪人力短缺，轉而招募外國人。犯罪集團特別相中台灣人，主因在於年輕人對日本戒心極低，且享有免簽證待遇，犯案後能迅速離境使警方難以追查。對集團而言，這些不會日語、僅靠翻譯軟體出面取款的車手純屬「拋棄式工具人」，即便被逮也不會危及核心組織。

犯罪版圖延伸毒品走私：付出沉重代價的三大族群

除了詐騙，近年台灣人涉嫌在日走私毒品的案件亦時有所聞，例如有年輕女性受社群徵才利誘，將新興毒品「依托咪酯」偽裝成威士忌託運入關遭逮。作者強調，犯罪集團將風險完全轉嫁，最終付出慘痛代價的包括三類人：首先是被招募的嫌犯，在日本恐面臨嚴格徒刑甚至終身不得入境；其次是遭詐騙的受害者，多數是積蓄被洗劫一空的長輩；最後則是全體台灣觀光客，日本預計於2028年實施更嚴格的事前入境審查，少數人的犯罪行為恐重創台灣旅客的國際形象。

================================================

Taiwanese people love traveling to Japan. Last year, the number of visitors reached 6.76 million. Just how many people is that? Ten years ago, it was only about 3 million. Look at how fast that growth is! But, some people originally went for travel, yet ended up becoming fraud offenders, and their numbers are increasing. In just these two months, there have been at least four cases involving Taiwanese. Some acted as money mules, while others posed as police officers to swindle money, with amounts ranging from hundreds to tens of millions of yen. These are just the ones caught; there's. no telling how many weren't. It's truly a global embarrassment. Many suspects claimed they saw ads online for " overseas travel part-time jobs, earn money while having fun." Some even realized it was illegal upon arriving in Japan, but proceeded because they were told foreigners wouldn't face serious consequences if caught. According to Ministry of Foreign Affairs statistics, the number of Taiwanese involved in fraud cases in Japan was four in 2023, but it surged to 50 in 2025. Why do transnational. criminal syndicates like targeting Taiwanese so much? Hello everyone, I’m Fan Fei. Welcome to "Fan Fei Looks at the World." First, let’s take a look at who these criminal syndicates recruiting people really are . Judging from exposed cases, the ringleaders come from several places. Besides local Japanese Yakuza, there are nomadic criminal groups from China, Taiwanese groups that shifted operations to Japan due to crackdowns at home, and fraud bases jointly operated by Japanese and Chinese handlers. According to Japan's National.

Police Agency, the number of foreigners caught in similar special fraud cases reached 236 in 2025, nearly doubling from the previous year. The proportion of foreigners in total cases rose from 5.7%to 10.2%, showing a clear increase in foreigners committing such fraud in Japan. Among the foreigners caught, the majority are from China and Vietnam, while numbers from Taiwan and Malaysia are also trending upward. The jobs these people are assigned are almost identical: showing up to collect cash. Being seen in front of security cameras is also why they are most easily caught . Why are there more and more Taiwanese ? Japanese media analyzed a few reasons . First, syndicates lack manpower, and Taiwanese are the easiest to recruit. Experts point out that with Japan’s aging population, low birth rate, and the government’s strengthened awareness campaigns, local criminal labor has decreased, so syndicates turned to foreigners. Why specifically Taiwanese? Taiwanese police analyze that fraud groups target young people in their 20s and 30s who are short on money, and Taiwanese are uniquely. low-guarded against Japan. The Ministry of Foreign Affairs points out that while Taiwanese people have high awareness of scams in Southeast Asia, ads for "free trips" or "jobs in Japan" still lure many. What's worse is that once you hand over your passport, photos, and address, it's difficult to back out. A former Taiwanese suspect once claimed that the scammers threatened him, insisting he must go to Japan and could not refuse, otherwise ...Secondly...Visa-free entry, strike once they succeed, then leave. Japanese police note that criminal syndicates.

exploit visa-free convenience, targeting these countries with ads. Once these recruits enter and collect cash, they leave immediately, leaving police with no leads. This has become the source of what Japan now calls " dark part-time jobs." Japanese scholars analyze that since there are so many tourists, syndicates believe blending foreign couriers among them is undetectable. They also warn that this tactic of using tourism to cover up crimes may become increasingly rampant. For instance, a 23-year-old Taiwanese. man caught in March went to Japan as a courier under the guise of tourism. The syndicate posed as police to intimidate the victim, claiming they were involved in fraud and had to pay to "cooperate with the investigation" or face arrest. The Taiwanese courier collected 6.59 million NTD from the victim and left the country. The victim only reported it after hearing nothing further. Police identified him via surveillance footage but only arrested him upon his re-entry to Japan. If he hadn't returned to Japan, he might never have. been caught. Moreover, not speaking Japanese is no obstacle; many Taiwanese couriers speak zero Japanese. They just show fake IDs and use translation apps, making them disposable and impossible to trace back to the ringleaders. To the syndicates, these couriers are " disposable." Even if arrested, it doesn't hurt them. As long as one out of ten succeeds, it's enough. Mainichi Shimbun reported that scammers increasingly use multi-person relay tactics to launder money. They recruit.

extensively from overseas, with each person handling only a small segment, making it even harder for police to trace the chain. In short, criminal syndicates are looking for "tools"— people who can get in and out quickly, are easily replaceable, and can't lead police back to them if things go wrong. Taiwanese enjoy visa-free entry to Japan, are familiar with the environment, and lack caution regarding Japanese legal risks, perfectly fitting these requirements. Beyond fraud, another major area for Taiwanese involvement in crimes in Japan in recent years is drug smuggling. This. September, a 23-year-old Taiwanese woman attempted to smuggle the synthetic drug "Etomidate" from Malaysia into Japan. She hid three kilograms of the substance, disguised as whiskey in bottles, inside her checked luggage, but was caught by customs officials at Narita Airport. Police arrested the woman for violating the Act on Securing Quality, Efficacy and Safety of Products Including Pharmaceuticals and Medical Devices. She claimed to police that she had applied for the job after seeing a. recruitment post on social media and was unaware of the contents. Etomidate is classified as a Schedule 1 controlled substance in Taiwan, and Japan’s Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare designated it as a prohibited substance last year. However , criminal syndicates push all the risks onto others, and the ones who truly pay the price are three specific groups of people. The first group is those recruited to commit the crimes. As mentioned, Taiwanese couriers often think foreigners won't face serious consequences if caught, assuming it's.

just deportation. They are wrong. Japan's drug laws can carry 10-year sentences; even couriers who just collect money can be sentenced directly , and drug trafficking carries even harsher penalties. Japan has strict laws against the smuggling, sale, possession, and use of various drugs. Depending on the severity, penalties range from a minimum of one year in prison to life imprisonment, and those sentenced to over a year of imprisonment are strictly punished. In principle, they will be barred from entering Japan. "I didn't know what was inside" is not a valid excuse to escape. legal responsibility. The second group is the victims. Japanese police state that money stolen in these scams is rarely recovered. The syndicate profits from a single success, while the victims bear the loss alone. Many victims are elderly, and the stolen money is often their retirement savings , which is nearly impossible to earn back. Many victims blame themselves and are afraid to tell their families; these harms cannot be undone simply by catching a courier. The third group is us, the average tourists. These cases. have created an impression that foreigners threaten Japan's public safety, prompting Japan to tighten border controls. A new system is expected to launch in 2028; even travelers from visa-exempt countries will be required to provide details like accommodation and travel plans for advance screening. The actions of a few may add hurdles for all Taiwanese visiting Japan and damage the image of Taiwanese people there. For many Taiwanese, Japan is a familiar country they can visit at a moment's notice.

But when you see online ads offering free trips to Japan, simple work, and high pay, you really need to think twice. I really don't have much sympathy for these criminals. Whether they're acting as money mules or smuggling drugs, haven't the warnings over these past few years been enough? Who would actually believe someone who still claims they didn't know they were participating in a scam or didn't know they were carrying illegal drugs? Getting locked up is just what they deserve. On top of that, Japanese society is already pushing back strongly against overtourism, so adding these transnational crimes is just pouring salt in the wound. We always. feel that going to Japan is as familiar as visiting a neighbor, but a few bad apples will eventually spoil the whole bunch. With more and more news of Taiwanese committing crimes in Japan, do you think this will worsen the Japanese perception of Taiwanese tourists in the future? Or have you also seen these dark recruitment ads while scrolling on your phone that promise you can travel and make money at the same time? Feel free to leave a comment below and let me know.   • 了解海外違法對個人法律後果、高齡受害者家庭以及未來台灣人赴日觀光入境審查帶來的嚴重衝擊。

摘要

台灣人赴日犯罪激增：從觀光熱潮到跨國詐騙

作者指出，台灣人熱愛前往日本旅遊，但近年卻出現越來越多以觀光名義赴日從事詐騙的案例。光是近兩個月就至少發生四起台灣人涉案事件，金額從數百萬到數千萬日圓不等。根據外交部統計，台灣人在日本涉及詐騙的人數從2023年的4人暴增至2025年的50人。許多嫌犯受到網路上「海外打工兼旅遊、邊玩邊賺錢」的廣告吸引，甚至誤信「外國人被抓不會有事」的謊言，淪為犯罪組織的棋子。

犯罪集團的盤算：為何台灣人成為「闇黑打工」首選目標？

作者分析，幕後主謀涵蓋日本黑道、中國犯罪團夥以及自台灣轉移陣地的詐騙集團。日本因高齡少子化與政府強力宣導，本土犯罪人力短缺，轉而招募外國人。犯罪集團特別相中台灣人，主因在於年輕人對日本戒心極低，且享有免簽證待遇，犯案後能迅速離境使警方難以追查。對集團而言，這些不會日語、僅靠翻譯軟體出面取款的車手純屬「拋棄式工具人」，即便被逮也不會危及核心組織。

Taiwanese people love traveling to Japan. Last year, the number of visitors reached 6.76 million. Just how many people is that? Ten years ago, it was only about 3 million. Look at how fast that growth is! But, some people originally went for travel, yet ended up becoming fraud offenders, and their numbers are increasing. In just these two months, there have been at least four cases involving Taiwanese. Some acted as money mules, while others posed as police officers to swindle money, with amounts ranging from hundreds to tens of millions of yen. These are just the ones caught; there's. no telling how many weren't. It's truly a global embarrassment. Many suspects claimed they saw ads online for " overseas travel part-time jobs, earn money while having fun." Some even realized it was illegal upon arriving in Japan, but proceeded because they were told foreigners wouldn't face serious consequences if caught. According to Ministry of Foreign Affairs statistics, the number of Taiwanese involved in fraud cases in Japan was four in 2023, but it surged to 50 in 2025. Why do transnational. criminal syndicates like targeting Taiwanese so much? Hello everyone, I’m Fan Fei. Welcome to "Fan Fei Looks at the World." First, let’s take a look at who these criminal syndicates recruiting people really are . Judging from exposed cases, the ringleaders come from several places. Besides local Japanese Yakuza, there are nomadic criminal groups from China, Taiwanese groups that shifted operations to Japan due to crackdowns at home, and fraud bases jointly operated by Japanese and Chinese handlers. According to Japan's National.

Police Agency, the number of foreigners caught in similar special fraud cases reached 236 in 2025, nearly doubling from the previous year. The proportion of foreigners in total cases rose from 5.7%to 10.2%, showing a clear increase in foreigners committing such fraud in Japan. Among the foreigners caught, the majority are from China and Vietnam, while numbers from Taiwan and Malaysia are also trending upward. The jobs these people are assigned are almost identical: showing up to collect cash. Being seen in front of security cameras is also why they are most easily caught . Why are there more and more Taiwanese ? Japanese media analyzed a few reasons . First, syndicates lack manpower, and Taiwanese are the easiest to recruit. Experts point out that with Japan’s aging population, low birth rate, and the government’s strengthened awareness campaigns, local criminal labor has decreased, so syndicates turned to foreigners. Why specifically Taiwanese? Taiwanese police analyze that fraud groups target young people in their 20s and 30s who are short on money, and Taiwanese are uniquely. low-guarded against Japan. The Ministry of Foreign Affairs points out that while Taiwanese people have high awareness of scams in Southeast Asia, ads for "free trips" or "jobs in Japan" still lure many. What's worse is that once you hand over your passport, photos, and address, it's difficult to back out. A former Taiwanese suspect once claimed that the scammers threatened him, insisting he must go to Japan and could not refuse, otherwise ...Secondly...Visa-free entry, strike once they succeed, then leave. Japanese police note that criminal syndicates.

exploit visa-free convenience, targeting these countries with ads. Once these recruits enter and collect cash, they leave immediately, leaving police with no leads. This has become the source of what Japan now calls " dark part-time jobs." Japanese scholars analyze that since there are so many tourists, syndicates believe blending foreign couriers among them is undetectable. They also warn that this tactic of using tourism to cover up crimes may become increasingly rampant. For instance, a 23-year-old Taiwanese. man caught in March went to Japan as a courier under the guise of tourism. The syndicate posed as police to intimidate the victim, claiming they were involved in fraud and had to pay to "cooperate with the investigation" or face arrest. The Taiwanese courier collected 6.59 million NTD from the victim and left the country. The victim only reported it after hearing nothing further. Police identified him via surveillance footage but only arrested him upon his re-entry to Japan. If he hadn't returned to Japan, he might never have. been caught. Moreover, not speaking Japanese is no obstacle; many Taiwanese couriers speak zero Japanese. They just show fake IDs and use translation apps, making them disposable and impossible to trace back to the ringleaders. To the syndicates, these couriers are " disposable." Even if arrested, it doesn't hurt them. As long as one out of ten succeeds, it's enough. Mainichi Shimbun reported that scammers increasingly use multi-person relay tactics to launder money. They recruit.

extensively from overseas, with each person handling only a small segment, making it even harder for police to trace the chain. In short, criminal syndicates are looking for "tools"— people who can get in and out quickly, are easily replaceable, and can't lead police back to them if things go wrong. Taiwanese enjoy visa-free entry to Japan, are familiar with the environment, and lack caution regarding Japanese legal risks, perfectly fitting these requirements. Beyond fraud, another major area for Taiwanese involvement in crimes in Japan in recent years is drug smuggling. This. September, a 23-year-old Taiwanese woman attempted to smuggle the synthetic drug "Etomidate" from Malaysia into Japan. She hid three kilograms of the substance, disguised as whiskey in bottles, inside her checked luggage, but was caught by customs officials at Narita Airport. Police arrested the woman for violating the Act on Securing Quality, Efficacy and Safety of Products Including Pharmaceuticals and Medical Devices. She claimed to police that she had applied for the job after seeing a. recruitment post on social media and was unaware of the contents. Etomidate is classified as a Schedule 1 controlled substance in Taiwan, and Japan’s Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare designated it as a prohibited substance last year. However , criminal syndicates push all the risks onto others, and the ones who truly pay the price are three specific groups of people. The first group is those recruited to commit the crimes. As mentioned, Taiwanese couriers often think foreigners won't face serious consequences if caught, assuming it's.

just deportation. They are wrong. Japan's drug laws can carry 10-year sentences; even couriers who just collect money can be sentenced directly , and drug trafficking carries even harsher penalties. Japan has strict laws against the smuggling, sale, possession, and use of various drugs. Depending on the severity, penalties range from a minimum of one year in prison to life imprisonment, and those sentenced to over a year of imprisonment are strictly punished. In principle, they will be barred from entering Japan. "I didn't know what was inside" is not a valid excuse to escape. legal responsibility. The second group is the victims. Japanese police state that money stolen in these scams is rarely recovered. The syndicate profits from a single success, while the victims bear the loss alone. Many victims are elderly, and the stolen money is often their retirement savings , which is nearly impossible to earn back. Many victims blame themselves and are afraid to tell their families; these harms cannot be undone simply by catching a courier. The third group is us, the average tourists. These cases. have created an impression that foreigners threaten Japan's public safety, prompting Japan to tighten border controls. A new system is expected to launch in 2028; even travelers from visa-exempt countries will be required to provide details like accommodation and travel plans for advance screening. The actions of a few may add hurdles for all Taiwanese visiting Japan and damage the image of Taiwanese people there. For many Taiwanese, Japan is a familiar country they can visit at a moment's notice.

But when you see online ads offering free trips to Japan, simple work, and high pay, you really need to think twice. I really don't have much sympathy for these criminals. Whether they're acting as money mules or smuggling drugs, haven't the warnings over these past few years been enough? Who would actually believe someone who still claims they didn't know they were participating in a scam or didn't know they were carrying illegal drugs? Getting locked up is just what they deserve. On top of that, Japanese society is already pushing back strongly against overtourism, so adding these transnational crimes is just pouring salt in the wound. We always. feel that going to Japan is as familiar as visiting a neighbor, but a few bad apples will eventually spoil the whole bunch. 摘要

疫情留下的復航難題

石垣島位於沖繩，距離台灣不遠，從桃園搭機約一小時即可抵達。疫情期間，島上醫療資源有限，居民曾呼籲旅客暫勿前往，觀光人潮因此大幅減少，國際航線停飛，相關地勤與行李服務業者也相繼撤離。日本重啟國際觀光後，航空公司雖有意復飛，石垣機場卻缺乏協助卸載行李、引導飛機及服務旅客的人手，航線因此難以恢復。

辭去銀行工作，押上一切創業

熱愛飛機、原本在銀行工作的作者受訪對象 Ryosuke，明白國際航班對仰賴觀光的石垣島有多重要。2023年8月，他決定親自投入地勤服務；隔年3月，年僅29歲的他創立公司，並貸款約兩億日圓添購設備。創業資金很快見底，他一度只剩一千日圓，為了籌錢還將愛車低價賣給朋友。即使身為丈夫與父親，他仍選擇冒險，希望為家鄉帶來新的發展機會。

親自拜訪航空公司，逐一跨過門檻

為了找回國際航班，Ryosuke 親赴那霸機場，逐一拜訪航空公司櫃檯、遞上名片並介紹石垣島。真誠與積極的態度讓韓國真航空注意到他，雙方後來促成與石垣市政府的合作，並啟動航線計畫。復航還必須解決航空保安人員經驗不足的問題，他透過人脈找到關西地區的相關公司，再親自說明、爭取合作。至於航空公司設立機場辦公室所遇到的合約與許可「雞生蛋、蛋生雞」困局，他則以航空公司出具的合作意向書作為折衷方案，成功推動程序。

讓孩子看見更大的世界

Ryosuke 並非石垣島出身，而是來自附近人口僅約兩百人的小濱島。他曾坦言，求學時連離開沖繩都缺乏勇氣，更不敢想像出國。這段經歷使他希望島上的孩子長大後，能自然地把出國視為一種選擇，不再覺得外面的世界遙不可及。他創立的公司如今除了負責飛機引導與行李處理，也提供英語、韓語旅客服務，並持續協助招攬新航線、增加航班。

觀光成長與地方生活的平衡

Ryosuke 的故事也映照出日本觀光發展的落差：京都等熱門地區承受過度觀光壓力，許多地方城市卻仍盼望旅客到訪。日本入境旅客屢創新高，但住宿旅客高度集中於少數都道府縣，觀光資源分布並不平均。石垣島在2025年迎來約149萬名旅客，創下新高，居民也開始擔心交通、基礎設施與自然環境受到負擔。當地預計自2027年起徵收住宿稅，盼將部分觀光收益用於改善環境，讓旅遊發展與居民生活共存。Ryosuke 最令人佩服之處，在於沒人敢承擔風險時，他選擇踏出最艱難的第一步；至於如何讓觀光利益留在地方、同時維護生活品質，仍需要政府、業者與居民共同努力。

Wild cats were drawn to. the rodents, and humans realized cats. were good at catching them, which is. how cats entered human life. formed a mutually beneficial. relationship in environments created by. humans, rather than being captured and. trained from the start. The second is time; dogs. require regular walks and outdoor. activities, which is very demanding for. office workers with long hours. The. third is the different emotional. responses needed from pets. A study. asked 520 self-identified "cat people" why they like cats; the word " independent" appeared 139 times, often. linked to being "easier to care for."

As mentioned earlier, through long-term. domestication, dogs have increasingly. focused their attention on humans,. often relying on them for a sense of. security. When owners disappear for. eight or nine hours every day, it can. affect the emotional state of some dogs. . After the owner leaves, dogs often. display separation-related behaviors. like whimpering, pacing, destroying. items, or even having accidents indoors. . This may be rooted in fear,. frustration, or boredom, but British. research indicates that such issues are. linked to a dog's welfare; since they. often occur when owners are away, they. are easily underestimated. Because. their ancestors were solitary, they. didn't enter human society to follow. orders, so their daily activities don't. require the same immediate human. response as dogs. In urban settings,. this matters; we want companionship but. lead busy lives. Research Center survey of 3,000. American pet owners found that 97%. consider their pets to be family. Over.

half even believe they are as important. as human family members, and in urban. areas, that figure exceeds 60%, turning. our furry friends into big business. our emotions. But now, many young. people feel there's no need to raise. children; their cats or dogs are their. family. They spend a lot of effort. building a life together, and small and. big, again see you.
